h1: Garlic Infused Olive Oil, and How to Make It Safely
excerpt: Garlic infused olive oil is easy to make and easy to make badly, because garlic sealed under oil at room temperature is a recognised botulism risk. Here is the safe way, the fridge window, and what to do with the jar.
keyTakeaway: Garlic infused olive oil must be refrigerated the moment it is made, strained clear of every clove, and used within three or four days. Fresh garlic is a low-acid vegetable, and sealed under oil at room temperature it grows the toxin behind botulism. Never leave the jar on the counter.

intro: Before the recipe, the rule that decides whether the recipe is worth making: garlic sitting in oil at room temperature is a botulism risk, and no amount of good olive oil changes that.
Fresh garlic is a low-acid vegetable. Sealed under oil it loses its air, and low-acid plus airless is what Clostridium botulinum needs. Make it, chill it, strain it, finish it within days.

sections.heading: The safety rule comes before the flavour

blocks.text: Fresh garlic is a low-acid vegetable, and sealed under olive oil at room temperature it creates the oxygen-free, low-acid conditions Clostridium botulinum needs to produce its toxin, and botulism is a medical emergency when it happens. Nothing in the taste or smell would warn a cook. Home-made garlic oil belongs in the refrigerator, the one exception to the never-refrigerate rule for plain oil, never the counter.

items: **Never store it at room temperature.** Not overnight, not an afternoon beside the hob.
**Never leave the garlic in the jar.** Strain out every clove and every fragment.
**Never stretch the window.** Date the jar and throw out what is older.
**Never give a jar away** — a gift travels warm.

sections.heading: Why a shop bottle is not the same thing

blocks.text: Commercial garlic oils are acidified to a controlled pH, or built from distilled garlic flavour rather than raw cloves, under a validated process. A home kitchen cannot hold that acidity in a jam jar, so a shelf-stable bottle in a shop argues nothing for yours.

sections.heading: Cold infusion against gentle warm infusion

blocks.text: Cold infusion means peeled cloves steeping in oil in the fridge, giving a clean, raw, slightly sharp garlic note after about a day. Warm infusion means cloves held in oil over low heat for twenty minutes, giving a rounder, sweeter flavour the same evening. Both need refrigerating.

sections.heading: A step by step method for a small jar

blocks.text: One small jar at a time is the right scale, because the window is short and a big batch only guarantees waste. Six to eight peeled cloves to 250 ml of extra virgin olive oil is a workable ratio. Have the strainer ready before the pan goes on.

items: Wash and dry a small glass jar and its lid.
Peel six to eight cloves and leave them whole; chopped garlic sheds fragments a strainer misses.
Warm 250 ml of olive oil with the cloves on the lowest heat for twenty minutes, or steep cold in the fridge overnight.
Keep it at a bare shimmer. Bubbling means frying, and fried garlic turns the oil bitter.
Strain through a fine sieve, then through muslin, until no solids remain.
Cool, cap, label with the date and refrigerate straight away.

sections.heading: Straining, chilling, and knowing when to throw it out

blocks.text: The garlic must come out because the solid clove is the part that holds a low-acid, airless pocket under the oil, and it is also what turns the flavour sharp and muddy by the second day. Strain twice, chill immediately, and treat a few days as the whole life of the jar.

Chilled olive oil clouds and thickens, and that alone is normal. Bubbles rising in a still jar, a hissing or bulging lid, a sour smell, or unstrained cloves gone soft and grey are not. Throw that jar away.

sections.heading: What to pour it on, and the infusions this shop does sell

blocks.text: Garlic oil is a finishing oil. Pour it over pasta the moment it leaves the pan, over roast potatoes, grilled vegetables or a bowl of soup, and onto warm bread. Add it off the heat so the aroma survives, then return the jar to the fridge.

Make a small jar, cold or gently warmed, strain every scrap of garlic out, refrigerate it once cool and finish it within days. Garlic left under oil on a counter is the version to refuse.

faqs.q: Is it safe to make garlic infused olive oil at home?
faqs.a: Yes, if you refrigerate it at once, strain the garlic out and use it within three or four days. Garlic under oil at room temperature is a botulism risk; the counter is never an option.

faqs.q: How long does home-made garlic olive oil keep?
faqs.a: Three or four days in the refrigerator, and that is the whole window. Freeze it in an ice tray for longer. Write the date on the jar, and discard any jar that spent an hour warm.

faqs.q: Does heating the garlic make the oil safe to store?
faqs.a: No. Gentle warming draws out flavour but it does not acidify the garlic or sterilise the jar, so a warm infusion needs the same refrigeration and the same few-day window as a cold one.

faqs.q: Why must the garlic be strained out?
faqs.a: Solid garlic under oil is what creates the low-acid, airless pocket, and it is also what turns the flavour sharp and muddy. Straining twice removes it and keeps the finished oil clear.

faqs.q: How do I tell garlic oil has turned?
faqs.a: Look for bubbles in a still jar, a lid that hisses or bulges, a sour or yeasty smell, or unstrained cloves gone soft and grey. Throw the jar out rather than tasting it.
